1 big thing: Blue wave math
 
Data: The Downballot and Sabato's Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia Center for Politics. Map: Kavya Beheraj/Axios

Redistricting has helped House Republicans build a seawall that can withstand a roughly 5-point Democratic wave.

  • Why it matters: Early readings are pointing to something twice that size — enough to wash away the GOP House majority, Axios' Hans Nichols reports.

Democrats have been running roughly 10 points ahead of their 2024 presidential performance in special elections this year.

  • A swing of that magnitude would produce a comfortable 230-205 Democratic majority, according to an Axios analysis of how the battle for the House would play out under different electoral scenarios.

🖊 Between the lines: Gerrymandering since the presidential election has given Republicans more breathing room, with GOP-drawn maps creating a net advantage of roughly nine seats.

  • But some of those newly redrawn GOP seats rest on a potentially shaky assumption: that the 2026 electorate will look much like that of 2024.
  • A national swing toward Democrats like the one in Trump's first midterm would overwhelm the GOP's redistricting defenses.

The other side: If Republicans outperform Trump's 2024 numbers by 5 points across congressional districts, the new maps would give them a massive 253-182 majority.

  • If 2026 simply looks like 2024 — with GOP candidates winning every district Trump would've carried under the new maps, including Trump districts where Democrats held on in 2024 — Republicans would net 16 seats, producing a 236-199 majority.

🏛 State of play: Two months before Election Day, Democrats can taste the House majority, provided two conditions hold: President Trump remains unpopular, and vulnerable Republicans stay close to him.

  • They're privately giddy that Republicans are encouraging vulnerable incumbents to attend this week's GOP midterm convention in Dallas and lash themselves to the mast of HMS Trump.

💰 Republicans are banking on their massive money advantage and a Supreme Court ruling that allows them to coordinate their campaign dollars with individual candidates.

2. 💡 Altman interview: Revenge of "idea guy"
 
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speaks Wednesday during the G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill, N.C. Photo: Matt Ramey/AFP via Getty Images

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says this era is bringing the revenge of the "idea guy" — the once-annoying aspiring entrepreneur burbling about their brainstorm with no technical chops to pull it off.

  • Altman says it would be like saying: "I have a great idea for a song. I just need that guy with the guitar to make it for me."
  • "It really did strike me as ridiculous," Altman told me in Chapel Hill, N.C. "But now we're watching a whole generation of people iterate on ideas faster than they ever could. The economics have been reset for what it means to make a new small business or large business."

👀 Why it matters: Polls show most Americans think the risks of AI outweigh the benefits, with data-center rage as a bipartisan bonfire in the midterms. Altman — who's trying to sell AI into a massive backlash — wants to remind Americans that amid all the real risks, AI can equal opportunity.

  • "This is gonna be the best time in the world to do a startup," Altman said recently.

Reality check: These new tools are great for idea people. But most people are doers, not dreamers, and don't feel they have the time or AI skills to spin up a startup in their spare time.

  • Our experience is that AI is a real unlock for a very small percentage of people who are idea generators or problem solvers, and in a position to put that into action.

📈 By the numbers: An American startup boom ignited during COVID and continued through this summer. Filings of new-business applications have continued to set records in the chatbot era.

  • The number of new U.S. businesses formed in the first half of this year, over 3 million, is the most for a January-June stretch in Census Bureau data going back to 2005.

The backstory: I first heard Altman's "idea guy" riff last spring, when he was talking onstage with Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, who asked how traits of successful founders were changing in this era.

  • "We would make fun of these [idea] people," Altman said. "They weren't that successful. And it was kind of always personally annoying to me. All of a sudden it's like the revenge of the idea guys."

🔎 That stuck in my mind. So when I sat down with Altman, 41, last week at the Carolina Inn in a bilateral meeting room during the G20 Innovation Ministerial, I asked him how that notion could be useful for today's AI users, or for people who should be wielding AI but are skeptics.

  • With GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI's powerful new model, Altman said, "you can start and run a small business effectively. ... It's like anyone who wants to have a company now has genius-level employees in every area of expertise."

Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI's chief scientist, posted 3,000 words on the state of AI yesterday, "An Alien Mind," with the stark warning: "The risks associated with AI are unfortunately going to grow from here. A very capable agent explicitly trained and instructed to carry out nefarious acts presents a new kind of danger ... "

  • "I expect and hope for voluntary slowdowns [by the labs] to become commonplace until shared safety bars are established." Keep reading.

3. 🗳️ GOP struggles in key gov races
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

With midterms 57 days away, a warning light is blinking for Senate Republicans: underperforming gubernatorial nominees in three crucial Midwest states — Michigan, Iowa and Ohio.

  • Why it matters: Strong candidates for governor can act as sheepdogs in tight Senate races, keeping Republican voters — and GOP-curious independents — moving in the party's direction, Axios' Hans Nichols reports.

👀 This is adding to GOP anxiety in Michigan and Iowa, where the Democratic gubernatorial nominees have led for much of the summer.

  • In Ohio — a state President Trump won by 11 points — the governor's race is tied.

The other side: The GOP is strong in several governor races.

  • Republicans are enthusiastic about Georgia, where the gubernatorial race between former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms (D) and health care executive Rick Jackson (R) is tight, but Jackson is expected to spend heavily in the final months.
  • In Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott (R) leads state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D) 47% to 44%, per 270toWin.
  • In New Hampshire, Gov. Kelly Ayotte (R) leads former Executive Councilor Cinde Warmington (D) by an average of 49% to 39%.

5. 🍳 AI is cookin'
 

Illustration: Tiffany Herring/Axios
 

Americans are deeply skeptical of virtually everything to do with AI — except when it comes to making dinner, Axios' Ben Berkowitz writes.

  • Why it matters: The AI industry has a giant problem with public perception that's only getting worse.

🍝 By the numbers: An NBC News poll of 7,105 American adults, out yesterday, asked what kinds of information they'd be comfortable getting from AI.

  • 74% said they'd trust AI for recipes, the only category where a majority were confident in what chatbots had to say.

⚠️ Stunning stat: Nothing else broke 34%, and some categories (like parenting advice or where to vote) didn't even top 20%.

🥣 Between the lines: AI actually has a pretty strong track record behind the stove, despite all the controversy over its other uses.

  • A Utah State University study last summer found people were equally willing to take cooking advice from AI as from nutrition students.

The intrigue: Aside from the recipe result, the rest of the NBC poll was pretty grim for AI — 73% said they were worried about misinformation, and 81% said the government wasn't doing enough to regulate the technology.

6. 🤖 AI's classroom reckoning
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

America's two largest school districts both imposed sweeping AI bans this past week, hitting the brakes on a technology that's rapidly making its way into classrooms around the country.

  • Why it matters: Some studies have found personalized AI tutors can improve learning. But other research has linked AI-assisted essay writing to weaker critical thinking, Axios' Josephine Walker reports.

🎒 New York City's public school district blocked AI use for roughly 600,000 students in pre-K through 8th grade and restricted it to specific uses in high school.

  • Hours later, Los Angeles Unified imposed a districtwide moratorium on AI use on school devices for this school year.

What we're watching: Chicago school board candidates have signed a pledge demanding a three-year moratorium on generative AI in the city's schools.

7. 🇩🇪 Far right's German jolt
 
Ulrich Siegmund, lead candidate of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, and his wife, Julia Siegmund, arrive to vote yesterday in Tangermünde, eastern Germany. Photo: Annegret Hilse/Reuters

Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a record 44% in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt yesterday, bringing the party closer than ever to forming Germany's first far-right state government since World War II, Axios' Andrew Pantazi writes.

  • The AfD fell just short of a majority. The election was only regional but has major national implications. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz had vowed to weaken the AfD. Instead, his party was crushed yesterday.

The AfD agenda includes heavy restrictions on immigration, restoring ties with Russia, cutting support to Ukraine and quitting the euro. (Reuters)

8. 🍿 1 film thing: Hollywood's banner summer
 
Matt Damon as Odysseus in "The Odyssey." Photo: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal Pictures via AP

It's a wrap on Hollywood's best summer in a decade.

  • After years of new-normal ticket sales and regular spells of unease, the summer box office rallied to $4.61 billion in domestic ticket sales between May 1 and Aug. 31, according to Rentrak.

🎟️ That's a 26.1% increase from 2025 and better than every summer other than 2013. Accounting for inflation and higher ticket prices, it's less of a record season, but 2026 was still the summer Hollywood got its mojo back. (AP)

Inde Navarrette and Michael Johnston in "Obsession." Photo: Focus Features via AP

Gen-Z audiences filled theaters and turned low-budget films, including "Obsession," into blockbusters.

Global ticket sales are up 15% compared with last year. Five movies have passed $1 billion in ticket sales, Bloomberg reports (gift link).

  • "Spider-Man: Brand New Day," the biggest movie of the summer, has grossed $2.4 billion worldwide.
  • No. 2 — "The Odyssey" — has made $1.63 billion.

🥊 Reality check: Higher ticket prices "disguise a deeper decline in attendance," the N.Y. Times notes. "From Jan. 1 through Aug. 16, domestic theaters sold an estimated 568.4 million tickets, down 30% from the same period in 2019, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. That amounts to roughly 248 million missing admissions." (Gift link)
